analysis.title: UBS Global: Core Views - Fade Defensives, Global Outlooks, Flow, EU Conf Feedback
key_insights: Desk view is to fade Defensives, with caveats. Healthcare and Staples are the best-performing sector baskets over 1M, and Defensives have outperformed Cyclicals by 11% in that period.
In Financials, there is frustration over Insurance outperforming Banks even though 3Q results showed no real operational momentum or incremental improvement in Insurance.

The UBS Global Outlooks point to cyclical expansion, earnings resilience and higher rates (reaffirmed by this week's CPI), which the author says is not a backdrop that favors Defensive outperformance.

Geopolitics remains a potential headwind after the US midterms, with little tangible progress on US-Iran or Russia-Ukraine and several Eurozone national elections. The author argues the bar to re-escalation with Iran has risen post-midterms, so the market has moved into a 'No war, No peace' period in which Oil and Rates likely stay structurally higher without breaking underlying economic strength.

UBS is overweight Healthcare, which tops UBS Equity Strategy's REVS rankings as BioPharma sales growth rises. The desk would fund it with Staples because Healthcare trades at about half Staples' P/E to sales growth. Healthcare is also seen as under-owned by institutions and generalists after MFN/MAHA, with ample single-stock catalysts into 2027, and as a hedge against AI/Tech.

UBS is underweight Staples. Its recent strength reflects the unwind of a consensus funding trade and a flight to safety rather than better fundamentals. Earnings scores, valuation and expected sales growth are all near the bottom 5% of their three-year histories.

The three UBS Equity outlooks (US, EU, EM) share the message that earnings and economic growth are resilient despite macro and policy risks. The recent US derating has created more attractive valuations, particularly where earnings revisions are strong. AI remains the dominant growth engine, but the outlooks call for selectivity and diversification beyond the narrow AI trade. Cyclicals, capex themes, financials and investment-activity exposures are preferred over defensive or consumer-sensitive areas.

Flows: the rebound is more hedge fund (HF) and positioning-led than long-only (LO)-sponsored. In the US, HFs drove the recovery through covering and re-grossing, then returned to de-risking around NVDA and funding-sensitive AI beta, while LOs kept monetizing strength.

APAC flows were more constructive but narrow. Foreign buying returned to Korean large caps and Taiwan blue chips and memory, with corporate buybacks and stabilization support. Selling continued in Taiwanese components and back-end testing and in selected Korean AI names. HK/China was quieter, with passive internet demand.

Europe showed the clearest LO re-engagement, with buying of selected weakness and demand in semis, industrials, banks, energy and resources. Turnover was subdued and flows two-way. HF deleveraging has eased and positioning can support further upside, but durable continuation needs broader LO sponsorship.

UBS European Conference (16th edition, London): record 1,700 investors and over 160 companies. Investors were cautious but not capitulating, with government debt the main anxiety. Two-thirds of audience participants expect government debt to end in some form of monetisation, and 63% believe western governments made false economic promises.

In the conference audience polls, most expect AI's disinflationary impact only after 2028. Rising leverage and private-credit stress topped the underestimated private-market risks. Nearly 88% said French sovereign spreads have yet to peak. A majority remained bullish on US equities and 62% backed equities as 2027's best-performing asset class.

Corporates at the conference said broad regional growth is lacking. Growth is concentrated in structural-capex sectors with visible demand and scarce capacity: grid, electrification, datacenter infrastructure, defence, energy infrastructure, industrial automation and mining. Companies serving these themes reported tight supply out to 2028/29.

Inflation was evident across sectors and most companies expect to pass some or all of it through. Pricing power may be scarce for competitively pressured sectors such as European autos and labour-heavy ones such as retail and delivery. With limited growth, companies are cutting fixed costs, rationalizing capacity and divesting non-core assets, and the consumer-facing sector is the busiest for M&A.

Almost no company mentioned high rates causing balance-sheet stress, and disposal proceeds would likely go back to shareholders. Banks have moved from balance-sheet repair to profitability, distributions and selective growth, and the three listed exchanges in attendance were positive on growth.
